items.prompt: Which term describes the process in which individuals with heritable traits that suit their environment tend to survive and reproduce more than others?

options.label: Genetic drift
Gene flow
Mutation
Natural selection

rubric: Natural selection is differential survival and reproduction based on heritable traits.
Drift is chance change, gene flow is movement of alleles, mutation is a source of new alleles.

items.prompt: What is the ultimate source of new alleles in a population?

options.label: Natural selection
Gene flow
Mutation
Genetic drift

rubric: Mutation creates new alleles.
Gene flow only moves existing alleles; selection and drift change frequencies, not create alleles.

items.prompt: What is the term for the movement of alleles between populations through migration and interbreeding?

options.label: Gene flow
Bottleneck
Speciation
Adaptation

rubric: Gene flow is allele movement between populations.
Bottleneck is a population size reduction; speciation is formation of new species.

items.prompt: In a phylogenetic tree, what does a branching point (node) represent?

options.label: A point where two species merged
A common ancestor from which lineages diverged
A mutation in a single individual
A species that went extinct

rubric: Nodes represent divergence from a common ancestor.
Merging is not shown in standard trees; nodes are not extinction events.

items.prompt: Which term names structures in different species that share a similar underlying anatomy because of common ancestry, such as a human arm and a bat wing?

options.label: Homologous structures
Vestigial structures
Convergent structures
Analogous structures

rubric: Homologous structures come from shared ancestry.
Analogous structures share function but not ancestry.

items.prompt: Which of the following are mechanisms of evolutionary change in populations? Select all that apply.

options.label: Gene flow
Individual learning of a skill
Mutation
Genetic drift
Individual growth during life

rubric: Drift, gene flow and mutation change allele frequencies in populations.
Learned skills and growth in an individual do not alter allele frequencies.

items.prompt: A biology student is reading about how new species form. The text says that when a population is split by a river or mountain range and the groups stop exchanging alleles, they may diverge over time. What is this type of speciation called?

options.label: Convergent evolution
Artificial selection
Allopatric speciation
Sympatric speciation

rubric: Allopatric speciation follows geographic separation.
Sympatric speciation occurs without geographic separation.

items.prompt: A population of beetles has green and brown individuals. Birds eat green beetles more often on brown soil. Over generations, what is the most likely change?

options.label: Brown alleles become more common because brown beetles survive and reproduce more
Green beetles turn brown because they need camouflage
Brown alleles become common because mutation targets the soil color
Beetles all become brown because the population needs to adapt

rubric: Selection favors heritable traits that raise survival and reproduction.
Distractors suggest need-driven or directed change, a common misconception.

items.prompt: Why is genetic drift generally stronger in small populations than in large ones?

options.label: Small populations mutate faster because they have fewer individuals
Chance events can change allele frequencies more when few individuals reproduce
Small populations have stronger selection pressure on every trait
Small populations receive more gene flow because they are close together

rubric: Random sampling error is larger with fewer individuals.
Mutation rate and selection strength do not depend on size this way.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the claim that evolution acts on populations rather than individuals?

options.label: Individuals change their genes during life to match the environment
Individuals keep their genes, while allele frequencies shift across generations in a group
Individuals evolve when they gain traits they use often
Individuals evolve whenever they move to a new habitat

rubric: Populations change in allele frequency over generations.
Distractors reflect Lamarckian ideas of individual change.

items.prompt: Two species of unrelated desert plants both evolved thick, water-storing stems. How is this best classified?

options.label: Common descent, where both inherited stems from one ancestor
Genetic drift, where chance made both plants develop stems
Convergent evolution, where similar pressures produce similar traits independently
Divergent evolution, where a shared ancestor split into two lineages

rubric: Similar traits in unrelated lineages from similar pressures indicate convergence.
Common descent would imply homology, which does not apply here.

items.prompt: What does it mean to say two species share a more recent common ancestor on a phylogenetic tree?

options.label: They have lived in the same habitat for longer
They look more alike than any other pair of species
Their lineages branch from a node closer to the tips than other species do
They appear nearer each other on the page regardless of branching

rubric: Relatedness depends on shared nodes, not on page order or appearance.
Distractors confuse tree layout and similarity with ancestry.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly describe natural selection? Select all that apply.

options.label: It can only favor traits that are already present in the population
It results in organisms becoming perfectly adapted
It produces traits because the organism needs them
It acts on variation that is heritable

rubric: Selection needs heritable variation and works on existing variation.
Need-driven change and perfection are common misconceptions.

items.prompt: A farmer sprays a field with an insecticide that kills 99% of aphids. A few survivors have a heritable resistance trait. Years later, most aphids in the field are resistant. How should this outcome be explained?

options.label: Resistant survivors reproduced more, so resistance alleles became common
The insecticide caused mutations that gave all aphids resistance
Aphids gradually learned to tolerate the insecticide and passed on that habit
Aphids developed resistance because they needed it to survive

rubric: Pre-existing variation was selected for by the insecticide.
Distractors suggest learning, directed mutation or need-based change.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why we say populations, not individuals, evolve by natural selection?

options.label: Individuals alter their genes during life to fit the environment, then pass those changes on to offspring
Individuals keep their genes for life; allele frequencies shift across generations in the population
Populations only evolve when every member dies and an entirely new species replaces them
Individuals with useful traits choose to change their offspring's genes before birth occurs

rubric: Selection changes allele frequencies across generations; an individual's genotype is fixed.
Distractors reflect Lamarckian or purposeful-change misconceptions.

items.prompt: Which process is the ultimate source of brand-new alleles in a population?

options.label: Acclimation
Mutation
Natural selection
Genetic drift

rubric: Mutation creates new alleles; other processes only change frequencies or move existing alleles.
Learners confuse selection or acclimation with the origin of variation.

items.prompt: Which description best matches genetic drift?

options.label: Movement of alleles between populations when migrating individuals breed in the new location
Appearance of new alleles from copying errors that occur during DNA replication in cells
Random change in allele frequencies caused by chance, strongest in small populations
Change in allele frequencies because individuals with better-suited traits leave more offspring behind

rubric: Drift is chance-based change in allele frequency, larger in small populations.
Distractors describe selection, gene flow and mutation.

items.prompt: On a phylogenetic tree, species X and Y join at a node that species Z does not share. What does this show?

options.label: X and Y have changed less since splitting from Z, so they look more alike
X and Y share a more recent common ancestor than either shares with Z
X and Y are more similar in appearance than either is to Z, by definition
X and Y descended from Z, which is an older species still living today

rubric: Relatedness on a tree is read from shared recent ancestry, not from appearance.
Distractors treat living taxa as ancestors or equate relatedness with similarity.

items.prompt: A human arm, a bat wing and a whale flipper have the same arrangement of bones despite different uses. How should these structures be classified?

options.label: Analogous structures, which evolved separately because the animals use them for similar functions
Vestigial structures, which have lost their original function and are slowly disappearing now
Convergent traits, which arose because the three animals live in the same kind of habitat
Homologous structures, inherited with modification from a common ancestor

rubric: Similar underlying structure with different functions indicates homology from common ancestry.
Distractors confuse homology with analogy, vestigiality or convergence.

items.prompt: Which conditions are required for natural selection to change a population's traits over generations? Select all that apply.

options.label: The population must be very small
Individuals vary in the trait
Variants differ in how many offspring they leave
Individuals develop the traits they need during their lifetime
The variation is at least partly heritable

rubric: Selection needs heritable variation and differential reproductive success.
Acquired needs and small size are not requirements; they reflect Lamarckian ideas or confusion with drift.

items.prompt: A hospital finds that an antibiotic that once cleared a bacterial infection now often fails. Lab tests show a few bacteria in earlier samples already carried a resistance allele. Which explanation best fits the evidence?

options.label: Resistant variants already existed and survived treatment, so they reproduced and became common
The antibiotic lost strength over time, so the survivors were simply the stronger bacteria
Each bacterium sensed the drug and mutated on purpose to become resistant to it
Bacteria gradually built up tolerance during treatment and passed that tolerance to offspring

rubric: Pre-existing resistant variants were selected by the drug, raising their frequency.
Distractors suggest directed mutation or acquired tolerance being inherited.

items.prompt: A population of 50 diploid individuals has 20 AA, 20 Aa and 10 aa. What is the frequency of allele A?
rubric: A copies = 2(20)+20 = 60 of 100 alleles = 0.6.
Distractors come from counting genotypes instead of alleles.

items.prompt: A recessive condition affects 4% of a population in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (q^2 = 0.04). What is the expected frequency of carriers (heterozygotes)?
rubric: Distractors come from using q or q^2 or p^2 instead of 2pq.

items.prompt: In a finch population, beak depth is heritable. A drought leaves mostly large, hard seeds. Predict the change in mean beak depth in the next generation.

options.label: It increases, since deep-beaked birds crack hard seeds and leave more offspring
It decreases, since smaller beaks need less food and so help birds last through drought
It increases only if the birds spend the drought exercising their beaks to widen them
It stays the same, since individual beaks do not change in response to drought

rubric: Heritable deeper beaks give a survival and reproductive advantage, so the mean rises.
Distractors reflect use-and-disuse ideas or wrongly predict no change or the wrong direction.

items.prompt: A tree is written in nested form as (((A,B),C),D). Which taxon is the outgroup, branching off first from the others?

options.label: A
C
B
D

rubric: D is outside all the nested groups, so it diverged first.
Learners often pick the first-listed or innermost taxon.

items.prompt: An island population has allele frequency p = 0.2. Each generation, 10% of breeders are migrants from the mainland, where p = 0.8. Ignoring other forces, what is p after one generation?
rubric: Distractors average the two populations or use a wrong weighting.

items.prompt: Which situations would be expected to cause strong genetic drift? Select all that apply.

options.label: A flood leaves only 12 survivors of a large population
Eight birds colonise a remote island and found a new population
Two large populations exchange many migrants each generation
A population of millions mates randomly with no losses
Disease reduces a population to 20 individuals for several generations

rubric: Bottlenecks, founder events and small sizes make chance effects on allele frequency large.
Large random-mating populations and heavy migration reduce drift.

items.prompt: A river is dammed, splitting one fish population into two lakes with no movement between them. Lake 1 has a fish predator; Lake 2 has none. Which prediction best follows from evolutionary principles?

options.label: Both populations will stay identical because they started with the same genes
Allele frequencies will diverge through different selection and drift, and may eventually lead to reproductive isolation
Both will evolve the same traits because they share the same ancestry
Reproductive isolation will appear as soon as the dam is finished

rubric: Without gene flow, different selection and drift cause divergence that can lead to speciation.
Distractors ignore divergence or assume speciation is instant.

items.prompt: A population has 30 AA, 50 Aa and 20 aa individuals. What is the frequency of allele A?
rubric: Allele A count = 2(30) + 50 = 110 of 200 copies, so 0.55.
Distractors use genotype frequency (0.30) or ignore heterozygotes.

items.prompt: An island population has allele frequency p = 0.20. The mainland has p = 0.60. Each generation, 10% of island breeders are migrants from the mainland. What is p on the island after one generation?
rubric: 0.26 comes from adding m times the difference to the wrong base; 0.40 is the midpoint.

items.prompt: Narrow-sense heritability of beak depth is 0.5. The population mean is 10 mm and the mean of the parents selected for breeding is 12 mm. What is the predicted offspring mean?

options.label: 11 mm
12 mm
14 mm

rubric: Breeder's equation: R = h^2 S = 0.5 x 2 = 1 mm, so the mean is 11 mm.
12 mm assumes full heritability; 10.5 mm misapplies the formula.

items.prompt: A tree is written as (((A,B),C),D). Which statement follows from this topology?

options.label: C shares a more recent common ancestor with A than D does
D is the oldest species because it branches off first
C is more closely related to D than it is to A
B is the ancestor of A because the two are adjacent

rubric: A and B join first, then C joins them, then D, so C is closer to A than D is.
Distractors treat tips as ancestors or read branching order as species age.

items.prompt: Two populations start with allele frequency 0.5 at a neutral locus, one with N = 20 and one with N = 2000. There is no selection, mutation or migration. After 50 generations, which is more likely to have lost one allele?

options.label: Both equally, because neutral alleles drift at the same rate
The N = 20 population, because sampling error each generation is larger
The N = 2000 population, because more individuals mean more mutations
Neither, because frequency stays at 0.5 without selection

rubric: Drift is stronger in small populations because random sampling of gametes causes bigger swings.
Distractors assume that drift is independent of size or that frequencies stay fixed without selection.

items.prompt: Which situations are examples of gene flow between populations? Select all that apply.

options.label: A new mutation arises in a single island lizard
Wind carries pollen from a crop field to a wild relative population
A storm randomly kills most of an island population
Several mainland lizards join an island population and breed there

rubric: Gene flow is the movement of alleles between populations through migration and breeding.
A new mutation adds variation and a random die-off is drift; neither moves alleles between populations.

items.prompt: A field team counts 1000 beetles in a large, randomly mating population assumed to be in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. The green colour is recessive, and 90 beetles are green. The team wants to know how many beetles are expected to be heterozygous carriers. What is the expected number?
rubric: q^2 = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Heterozygotes = 2pq = 0.42, which is 420 beetles.
490 is the expected number of homozygous dominant beetles (p^2); 90 confuses carriers with green beetles.

items.prompt: Researchers raise ten small replicate lines of flies in identical conditions and track one allele. Which observation would most strongly point to drift rather than selection?

options.label: Lines change in different, unpredictable directions, with bigger swings in smaller lines
Change is largest in the lines with the greatest number of breeders
All lines shift in the same direction at similar rates
The allele rises only in lines where survival is measurably higher

rubric: Random divergence among replicates, stronger at small size, is the signature of drift.
Parallel change or change tied to fitness suggests selection.

items.prompt: A tree has the topology ((A,B),(C,D)). A trait is present in A and C only. What does the most parsimonious reconstruction imply?

options.label: One gain in the common ancestor explains it with no further changes
A and C must be sister taxa, so the tree is wrong
The trait must be homologous because two species share it
At least two independent changes are needed on this tree

rubric: With A and C in different clades, two gains (or one gain plus losses) are needed, which means homoplasy.
Distractors ignore the tree structure or equate shared traits with common origin.

items.prompt: The sickle-cell allele stays at about 10% in malaria regions even though homozygotes are severely ill. Which explanation best accounts for this stable frequency?

options.label: Recurrent mutation alone regenerates the allele at about that frequency
Heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote, so selection maintains both alleles
Genetic drift has carried the allele up in all large regional populations
Recessive alleles cannot be removed because heterozygotes hide them

rubric: Heterozygote advantage produces a balanced polymorphism at an intermediate frequency.
Hiding in heterozygotes slows removal but does not explain a stable 10% level.

items.prompt: A student writes: "Ancestral beetles that burrowed developed stronger forelegs and passed them on, so burrowing beetles evolved." What is the central flaw?

options.label: Stronger forelegs would be selected against because they cost energy
Behaviour such as burrowing cannot be influenced by natural selection
Evolution acts only on whole species, never on lineages within them
Traits gained through use are not inherited, so heritable variation must already exist for selection to act

rubric: Acquired changes do not alter gamete DNA; selection needs pre-existing heritable variation.
Distractors misstate the level at which selection acts, rule out behaviour or invent a cost.

items.prompt: Two trees have the same branching pattern, but at one node the two descending branches are swapped left to right. What does this show?

options.label: They show different relationships because left taxa are more ancestral
They differ because right-hand taxa are more derived
They show identical relationships; only the drawing order differs
They differ because tip order shows the order of divergence

rubric: Branches can rotate around a node without changing relationships.
Distractors read tip order as time or degree of advancement.

items.prompt: Which observations support selection acting on a gene, rather than drift alone? Select all that apply.

options.label: Independent populations in similar environments show the same allele change
Allele frequency shifts match fitness differences measured in the field
The ratio of nonsynonymous to synonymous changes (dN/dS) is above 1
Two isolated populations differ in allele frequency at the gene
Neutral markers across the genome show the same reduced diversity

rubric: dN/dS above 1, parallel change and fitness-matched shifts are locus-specific signs of selection.
Differences between isolated populations or genome-wide patterns can be produced by drift or demography.

items.prompt: A team sequences a mosquito population and finds very low nucleotide diversity in a 200 kb region around an insecticide-resistance gene. Diversity is normal across the rest of the genome. Which explanation best fits this pattern?

options.label: A selective sweep, in which a favoured allele rose quickly and carried its linked variants with it
A high mutation rate in the region, which would raise diversity
A recent bottleneck, which would lower diversity at this region only
Gene flow from a large neighbour, which would add variation to the region

rubric: A local loss of diversity around a selected gene is the signature of a sweep through hitchhiking.
A bottleneck would reduce diversity genome-wide, while mutation and gene flow would add variation.

items.prompt: At one locus, the gene tree groups human with gorilla, but the genome-wide species tree groups human with chimpanzee. Which explanation best accounts for this single-locus discordance?

options.label: Chimpanzees evolved this locus faster, which changed their apparent ancestry at it
The species tree is wrong because one locus outweighs all the other loci combined
Ancestral polymorphism persisted through two close speciations and sorted differently
Gorillas and humans swapped this gene by recent horizontal transfer between them

rubric: Incomplete lineage sorting of ancestral alleles across closely spaced splits yields gene trees that differ from the species tree.
Distractors invoke horizontal transfer or rate change, which are unlikely for a single nuclear locus among these apes.

items.prompt: Allele frequency shifts by 0.05 in one generation in both a 30-beetle and a 30,000-beetle population. Which further observation would best favour selection over drift as the cause?

options.label: The new frequency is not exactly 0.5 in either of the two populations
The shift is larger in the 30-beetle population than in the large one
The shift has the same direction in many replicate large populations under the same pressure
The shift was detected using a sample of only a few beetles from each

rubric: Consistent direction across replicate large populations is unlikely under drift, whose changes are random and scale with 1/N.
A bigger shift in the small population is the expected signature of drift, not selection.

items.prompt: A sample pooled from a lake shows fewer heterozygotes than Hardy-Weinberg predicts at a neutral locus. Two unrecognised subpopulations differ in allele frequency. Which process best explains the deficit?

options.label: Random mating within one large population that is at equilibrium
Heterozygote advantage, which raises heterozygote frequency above expectation
The Wahlund effect: pooling subpopulations with different frequencies lowers heterozygosity
Recurrent mutation, which creates heterozygotes faster than drift removes them

rubric: Pooling structured subpopulations reduces observed heterozygosity relative to the pooled allele frequencies (Wahlund effect).
Heterozygote advantage would increase, not decrease, heterozygotes.

items.prompt: A gene has a gene-wide dN/dS of 0.3 across mammals, yet a few codons are suspected of positive selection. Why could the gene-wide value hide this?

options.label: Averaging over all codons lets many constrained sites outweigh a few sites with dN/dS above 1
Positive selection only acts on noncoding sequence, so dN/dS cannot detect it in genes
Synonymous changes are always rarer than nonsynonymous ones, which biases the ratio low
A dN/dS below 1 proves that no codon in the gene has ever had an adaptive change

rubric: Gene-wide dN/dS averages across sites; strong purifying selection at most codons masks a few positively selected ones.
Distractors treat the average as proof of absence or misstate how synonymous and nonsynonymous rates compare.

items.prompt: A parsimony tree groups two distantly related, rapidly evolving lineages as sisters, though anatomy and slow-evolving genes place them apart. What is the most likely cause of the artefact?

options.label: Parsimony cannot handle sequences that are longer than about one thousand sites
Many independent substitutions on long branches coincidentally match, creating false shared changes
Both lineages share a recent common ancestor that the slow genes failed to record
Slow-evolving genes always give misleading trees because they contain too few changes

rubric: Long-branch attraction: homoplastic changes on long branches are misread as shared derived characters.
Distractors dismiss the better-supported signal or blame sequence length rather than convergent substitutions.

items.prompt: Two plant populations differ in leaf thickness. Which observations would support local adaptation rather than drift as the cause of the difference? Select all that apply.

options.label: Trait divergence matches neutral marker divergence across all pairs of populations
Each population outperforms the other in reciprocal transplants at its home site
Trait divergence (Qst) exceeds divergence at neutral markers (Fst)
Thickness tracks an aridity gradient across several independent population pairs

rubric: Qst above Fst, home-site advantage and repeated environmental correlation all indicate selection.
Divergence that simply mirrors neutral markers is what drift and isolation alone would produce.

items.prompt: Blind cave fish occur in three caves. A tree built from nuclear markers places each cave population inside a different surface-dwelling clade, not with the other cave populations. Eye loss is similar across caves. What inference does the tree best support?

options.label: Surface fish evolved eyes separately several times, so the cave state is ancestral
The markers are uninformative, because blind fish cannot be placed on a tree
Eye loss arose independently in each cave from different surface ancestors, a case of convergence
One ancestral cave population lost its eyes, then migrants colonised the other caves

rubric: Cave populations nested in separate surface clades imply separate colonisations and independent eye loss.
A single loss followed by migration would make the cave populations cluster together on the tree.

items.prompt: A small isolated population shows inbreeding depression. Criteria: restore diversity quickly while keeping the risk of outbreeding depression low. Which management option best meets them?

options.label: Captive-breed only the least related individuals within the current small population
Introduce a few migrants from the nearest ecologically similar population
Keep the population isolated so local adaptations are never diluted by foreign alleles
Introduce many individuals from a distant population adapted to very different conditions

rubric: A few migrants from a similar nearby population raise diversity and mask deleterious alleles with little adaptive mismatch.
Distant sources risk outbreeding depression; isolation or within-population breeding does not add new alleles.

items.prompt: A critic claims that a complex eye cannot evolve gradually because a partial eye is useless. Which critique is best supported by evidence?

options.label: The claim is valid for eyes, but only because eyes arose before natural selection began
Living species show functional intermediates from light-sensitive patches to cup eyes, each improving fitness
Eyes are too complex to test, so the claim cannot be evaluated
Complex organs always arise through large single mutations that skip any intermediate forms

rubric: Functional intermediates in living taxa show that partial eyes are useful and selectable.
Distractors either decline to evaluate the claim or replace gradualism with unsupported saltation.

items.prompt: Researchers claim a human allele is under recent positive selection. Criterion: evidence must rule out demographic history as the sole explanation. Which evidence is strongest?

options.label: Reduced nearby diversity and long haplotypes beyond what demographic simulations of the population predict
The allele is more common in cities than in rural areas of one country
The allele is at high frequency in the population studied
The allele alters a protein sequence that is conserved in other primates

rubric: A sweep signature compared against a demographic null model separates selection from bottlenecks and drift.
High frequency alone is explained by drift; conservation or geography alone do not show recent selection.

items.prompt: You must infer a tree from sequences where some lineages have very long branches and rates vary among sites. Criterion: minimise systematic error. Which method is best justified?

options.label: Maximum parsimony, because it makes no assumptions about the evolutionary process
Distance matrices from raw proportion of differing sites, because they are fastest to run
Neighbour joining with no correction, because correction adds arbitrary parameters to data
Likelihood or Bayesian inference with a substitution model that allows rate variation among sites

rubric: Model-based methods can account for multiple hits and rate heterogeneity, reducing long-branch artefacts.
Parsimony and uncorrected distances are more prone to long-branch attraction.

items.prompt: A review states: "Taxon A branches off first in the tree, so it is primitive and shows only ancestral traits." Which critique is soundest?

options.label: The claim is sound, because the earliest branch always retains the ancestral state at every trait
The claim is sound only if the tree was inferred from morphology and not DNA
The claim fails because trees cannot show which lineage branched first in any case
The claim fails because the first-branching lineage has had as long as any other to accumulate derived traits

rubric: All extant lineages have evolved for equal time since the split; a basal position does not mean ancestral traits.
Distractors treat branching order as a measure of primitiveness or deny that trees show order.

items.prompt: A report argues that a trait is an adaptation shaped by selection because it currently helps survival. Which are valid criticisms of this reasoning? Select all that apply.

options.label: A current benefit proves selection produced the trait for that function
The trait may be a by-product of selection on another trait
The trait may be an exaptation that arose for a different function
Comparative or phylogenetic evidence of selection is still needed

rubric: Current utility does not show origin: exaptations, by-products and drift can all yield useful traits.
Testing adaptation needs historical or comparative evidence, so the claim that benefit proves selection is flawed.

items.prompt: A pest evolves resistance to a crop toxin. Resistance is recessive and the toxin kills susceptible homozygotes and heterozygotes. Criterion: delay resistance as long as possible. Which plan is best?

options.label: Plant a high-dose toxin crop with a nearby refuge of non-toxin plants so resistant survivors mate with susceptible pests
Plant only toxin crops and spray the toxin more often to remove any survivors
Plant a low-dose toxin crop everywhere so selection stays weak and uniform on all pests
Rotate between two toxin crops yearly, with no refuge, so no single allele is favoured

rubric: A high dose plus a refuge makes rare resistant survivors mate with susceptible refuge pests, giving susceptible heterozygotes.
Universal exposure or low doses speed the spread of resistance alleles.

items.prompt: A paper reports a gene-wide dN/dS of 0.6 across a phylogeny and concludes that positive selection is absent from the gene. Judge this conclusion.

options.label: Supported: a gene-wide dN/dS below 1 means every codon is under purifying or neutral evolution on every lineage.
Unsupported: dN/dS is uninformative in coding sequences because synonymous sites are always under strong selection too.
Unsupported: averaging over all codons and lineages can hide a few positively selected sites among many constrained ones.
Supported: a value of 0.6 is close enough to 1 to indicate neutrality, so positive selection cannot be occurring.

rubric: Gene-wide averages mask site- or branch-specific positive selection; site and branch models are needed.
Distractors treat a below-1 average as proof about every codon, or misstate what dN/dS measures.

items.prompt: About 20% of gene trees disagree with the species tree for three closely related species. The aim is to decide between incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) and introgression. Which observation best favours introgression?

options.label: Discordant loci cluster on one chromosome and the two minority topologies occur in equal numbers.
Discordant loci show coalescence times older than the species split, which ILS cannot produce.
Discordant gene trees are not evenly split, and one minority topology is far more common than the other.
Discordant gene trees exist at all, since ILS would leave every locus matching the species tree.

rubric: ILS predicts the two minority topologies are equally frequent; an asymmetry (ABBA vs BABA excess) signals gene flow.
Distractors misread ILS as producing no discordance or as excluding deep coalescence.

items.prompt: An allele gives a 0.5% additive fitness advantage (s = 0.005) in a population with effective size Ne = 50. Using the criterion that selection is effective when s clearly exceeds 1/(2Ne), judge its likely fate.

options.label: Selection will dominate, since any positive s eventually fixes the allele with certainty in a finite population.
Drift will largely override selection, since s is below 1/(2Ne) = 0.01, so fixation is only slightly likelier than neutral.
Drift is irrelevant here, since random allele frequency change only occurs in very large populations.
Selection will dominate, since s = 0.005 exceeds 1/Ne = 0.02 once population size is taken into account.

rubric: 1/(2Ne) = 0.01 exceeds s, so the allele behaves nearly neutrally and drift dominates.
Distractors assume advantageous alleles always fix, botch the arithmetic, or invert the size dependence of drift.

items.prompt: To date a phylogeny, a team fixes a node's age at exactly 50 Ma, the age of the oldest known fossil assigned to that clade. Judge this calibration choice.

options.label: Flawed: fossils cannot calibrate trees, because only substitution rates from living species can give divergence times.
Flawed: the fossil gives only a minimum age, so the node needs a lower bound with a soft prior allowing older ages.
Sound if the fossil is well preserved, because good preservation fixes the divergence time at the fossil age.
Sound: the oldest fossil is the best estimate of the node age, because fossils record when a lineage first appeared.

rubric: The oldest fossil is a minimum for the node age; the lineage almost certainly arose earlier.
Distractors treat first fossil appearance as the origin time or reject fossil calibration altogether.

items.prompt: A genome scan between two stickleback populations finds Fst peaks mainly in low-recombination regions, and the authors claim each peak marks local adaptation. Which critique is strongest?

options.label: Low-recombination regions have higher mutation rates, which lower Fst and make these peaks a conservative estimate.
Fst peaks are sampling artefacts and cannot reflect real allele frequency differences between the populations.
Fst can only be raised by gene flow, so the peaks show recent migration rather than any selection.
Linked selection such as background selection cuts diversity in low-recombination regions and inflates Fst without local adaptation.

rubric: Background selection and sweeps reduce local diversity, raising Fst in low-recombination regions regardless of local adaptation.
Distractors reverse the effect of gene flow on Fst or dismiss Fst as pure noise.

items.prompt: A team finds a pale-coat allele common in sand-dwelling mouse species and concludes it is an adaptation for camouflage. Which criticisms are valid before accepting this claim? Select all that apply.

options.label: Sand-dwelling species may share the trait through common ancestry, so they are not independent data points.
Pale coat may be a byproduct of pleiotropy with another trait that is the real target of selection.
The allele may have spread by drift or a founder event in a small population rather than by selection.
Because mutations are random, a trait that fits its environment cannot have arisen through selection.
Camouflage hypotheses are untestable, so no predation experiment could ever bear on the claim.

rubric: Drift, pleiotropic byproducts and phylogenetic non-independence all undermine a simple fit-to-environment inference.
The other two options misstate how selection acts on random mutation or wrongly call adaptive hypotheses untestable.

items.prompt: A parsimony tree of 12 insect orders places two parasitic lineages with extremely fast-evolving rDNA as sister groups, although fossils and morphology place them far apart. Bootstrap support for the grouping is 98%. Criteria: avoid systematic artefacts with the fewest extra assumptions. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Trust the grouping because high bootstrap support rules out systematic error as an explanation for the placement.
Suspect long-branch attraction; re-run with a model-based method and add slow-evolving taxa to break the long branches.
Accept the grouping, since shared rapid substitution is a synapomorphy that outweighs morphology and fossils.
Discard the rDNA and rely on morphology alone, since molecular data cannot resolve relationships among orders.

rubric: Long-branch attraction produces strongly supported but wrong groupings; better models and denser taxon sampling address it.
Distractors treat convergent rate as homology, abandon molecular data, or mistake bootstrap support for accuracy.

items.prompt: Two beetle populations produce few hybrids in the wild. Design a lab study to decide whether isolation is mainly prezygotic or postzygotic; the lab can run mating trials and rear offspring. Which design meets this?

options.label: Run choice mating trials with both mate types, then force crosses and measure F1 viability and fertility against within-population crosses.
Compare mtDNA divergence between populations, since greater divergence directly quantifies the strength of prezygotic barriers.
Force crosses only and count F1 viability, since failed matings are a form of postzygotic isolation.
Run choice trials only; if any hybrids are produced, the isolation is postzygotic by definition.

rubric: Separating mate choice from hybrid fitness needs both choice trials and forced crosses with proper controls.
Distractors measure only one stage, or substitute genetic distance or presence of hybrids for the barrier itself.

items.prompt: Plan a dating analysis for a clade whose substitution rates vary about tenfold among lineages. Available: three fossils giving minimum ages, and one maximum bound from a dated geological event. Which plan fits these constraints?

options.label: Use a relaxed clock with no calibrations, since rate variation makes fossil constraints redundant to the analysis.
Use a strict clock calibrated on the single oldest fossil and apply one rate to all lineages for consistency.
Use an uncorrelated relaxed clock with all four calibrations as soft bounds, then compare priors-only and leave-one-out runs.
Average pairwise distances across lineages and convert to time using one rate from the geological event.

rubric: Rate variation needs a relaxed clock, and several soft calibrations plus sensitivity checks make use of all the constraints.
Distractors ignore rate variation, collapse the data to one rate, or drop calibrations needed for absolute time.

items.prompt: You want to test whether adaptation of E. coli to a new carbon source is repeatable or contingent on earlier chance mutations. Frozen samples can be revived at any time. Which experimental design best answers this?

options.label: Found one line from many different clones and track it, comparing its fitness with the ancestor over time.
Run a few replicates in different media and compare final fitness, since variation among media shows contingency.
Found many replicate lines from one clone and replay replicates from frozen intermediate generations, comparing fitness and mutations.
Run one very large population and sequence it at the end, since large size guarantees the most probable path.

rubric: Replicates from one clone plus replays from earlier time points separate chance, history and repeatability.
Distractors confound genotype or environment with history, or lack replication.

items.prompt: A proposal to show introgression between two mouse species sequences mtDNA from 30 individuals per species and finds some shared haplotypes. What is the most important element missing from the design?

options.label: Measurements of hybrid morphology, since only phenotype can reveal whether gene flow has occurred.
A measure of mtDNA mutation rate, since shared haplotypes imply introgression only when that rate is zero.
Genome-wide nuclear data with a test for excess allele sharing, since mtDNA is one locus, affected by sorting and sex-biased dispersal.
More mtDNA individuals per species, since sample size is the only limitation on inferring gene flow.

rubric: A single maternally inherited locus cannot separate introgression from ILS or selection; genome-wide tests can.
Distractors add more of the same marker or substitute irrelevant measurements.

items.prompt: A 25-animal isolated population shows inbreeding depression. A larger population of the same subspecies with similar habitat lies 40 km away. Goal: raise fitness while limiting swamping and outbreeding depression. Which plan meets this?

options.label: Translocate a few unrelated animals from the nearby population each generation and monitor ancestry, fitness and heterozygosity.
Introduce many individuals from a distant, different species with high diversity to maximise heterozygosity quickly.
Take no action, since any gene flow into a small population replaces its local gene pool and removes adaptation.
Breed all 25 in captivity with equal family contributions, which halts inbreeding without needing any outside genes.

rubric: Limited migration from a close, ecologically similar source masks deleterious alleles without swamping or outbreeding depression.
Distractors over-introduce divergent genes, refuse gene flow, or only slow further inbreeding.

items.prompt: Design a comparative test that high haemoglobin oxygen affinity is an adaptation to altitude across bird species. Which elements must the design include? Select all that apply.

options.label: Control for confounders such as body mass and temperature that also affect oxygen needs.
A phylogeny-based analysis, such as contrasts or PGLS, to correct for shared ancestry among species.
Sampling only species from the highest altitudes, to maximise the contrast in the trait.
Several independent origins of high-altitude living among the sampled lineages.
Treating each species as an independent data point to maximise statistical power.

rubric: Valid inference needs ancestry correction, replicated independent transitions and control of confounders.
Sampling only extremes removes the comparison group, and treating species as independent ignores shared ancestry.

items.prompt: A cooperative plants Bt crops against a moth pest. Resistance is recessive and starts rare (about 0.001). Goal: delay resistance for many years; alternative pesticides are not allowed. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Rotate Bt and non-Bt crops across the whole farm each year, which halves the selection pressure overall.
Plant a high-dose Bt variety beside a non-Bt refuge so rare resistant homozygotes mostly mate with susceptible moths.
Plant Bt everywhere at high dose to kill nearly all moths and leave no resistant survivors to breed.
Plant Bt everywhere at moderate dose so heterozygotes survive and share the selection pressure across genotypes.

rubric: High dose plus refuge keeps susceptible alleles abundant, so heterozygotes die and resistant moths mate with susceptible ones.
Distractors let heterozygotes survive, leave no refuge, or use rotation that does not keep susceptible moths nearby.
